title: Debiased Counterfactual Generation via Flow Matching from Observations
claim: Applying a flow to samples from the observational distribution yields minimal, structured edits that shift an attribute toward its population distribution.
layout: 2 rows by 8 columns of face images, top-to-bottom comparison
description: A compact grid of face images from CelebA with two rows of eight columns. The top row shows samples from the observational distribution of female faces, and most have blonde or light hair. The bottom row shows the same faces after the deconfounding flow. Each column pairs a top face with a bottom face of the same identity, pose and background. The main changes are in hair colour, which turns darker brown or dark blond in several columns, while the faces, expressions and backgrounds stay nearly the same. The bottom row is slightly blurrier. There are no arrows, labels or annotations in the crop, so the eye goes to the paired columns and the hair-colour differences. Photos on white, black and coloured backgrounds give variety.
caption: Top: CelebA samples from distribution PY |Sex=Female, which over-represents HairColor = Blonde. Bottom: after applying the deconfounding flow, the samples are distributed according to the learned marginal counterfactual distribution PY (Female), under which HairColor follows its population distribution. Learning PY (Female) via a flow from PY |Sex=Female, only requires learning structured image edits rather than the entire image structure, resulting in improved distributional accuracy (see Figure 4, left). Note, the samples are not identified unit-level counterfactuals.
abstract: Estimating the full counterfactual distribution under an intervention is central to treatment risk assessment and counterfactual generation tasks. Existing approaches model the counterfactual distribution as a standalone generative target, without exploiting its relationship to the observational data. In this work, we show that under standard assumptions, observational distributions and marginal counterfactual distributions over outcomes are tightly linked: they have identical support and tail behavior, remain statistically close under weak confounding, and share any outcome features which are invariant to confounders. These properties motivate learning counterfactual distributions not from scratch, but via a deconfounding flow from the observational distribution. We formulate this problem via flow-matching and derive a semiparametrically efficient estimator based on a novel efficient influence function correction. We subsequently extend our estimator to target minimal-energy flows in high-dimensions, which we show can be especially simple targets between observational and counterfactual distributions. In experiments, deconfounding flows outperform existing debiased counterfactual distribution estimators, while also mitigating known failure modes of flow-based methods.
